# Advanced TypeScript {#sec-advanced-ts}

## Learning goals

This chapter covers the type features that make larger TypeScript codebases expressive: generics, indexed access, mapped types, conditional types, utility types, `satisfies`, `as const`, branded types, and declaration patterns.

## Generics

Generics let a function preserve type relationships between its inputs and outputs.

### The problem without generics

```ts
function firstBad(items: any[]) {
  return items[0]
  // Returns any — type information is lost at the call site.
}

const name = firstBad(["core", "schema"])
// name is any — we can assign it to anything, defeating type checking.
```

With `any`, the function works for any array but discards the element type. The caller gets no useful type information back.

### Using a type parameter

```ts
function first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
  // T is a placeholder for the caller's element type.
  // first(["a", "b"]) infers T as string.
  // first([1, 2, 3]) infers T as number.
  return items[0]
}
```

The angle brackets `<T>` introduce a type parameter. TypeScript infers `T` from the argument at each call site.

```ts
const name = first(["core", "schema"])
// TypeScript infers: T = string, so name is string | undefined.

const count = first([1, 2, 3])
// TypeScript infers: T = number, so count is number | undefined.
```

Each call site gets its own concrete type. This is the key benefit: the type relationship is preserved without repeating the annotation.

### Multiple type parameters

```ts
function pair<A, B>(a: A, b: B): [A, B] {
  return [a, b]
}

const p = pair("hello", 42)
// TypeScript infers: A = string, B = number, so p is [string, number].
```

Use multiple parameters when a function works with two independent types. The names `A`, `B`, `T`, `U`, `K`, `V` are conventional, but you can use descriptive names:

```ts
function createMap<Key extends string, Value>(key: Key, value: Value) {
  return { [key]: value } as Record<Key, Value>
}
```

### Generic constraints with `extends`

When a generic function requires a specific shape from `T`, use `extends` to constrain it:

```ts
type Identifiable = { id: string }

function byID<T extends Identifiable>(values: readonly T[]): Map<string, T> {
  // T must have an id field (property of Identifiable).
  const map = new Map<string, T>()
  for (const value of values) {
    map.set(value.id, value)
  }
  return map
}

// Works for any type that has id: string.
type SessionInfo = { id: string; title: string }
type UserInfo = { id: string; name: string }

const sessions = byID<SessionInfo>([{ id: "s1", title: "Fix tests" }])
// sessions is Map<string, SessionInfo>.
```

### Default type parameters

You can provide a default type that is used when inference is ambiguous:

```ts
function createArray<T = string>(length: number, value: T): T[] {
  return Array.from({ length }, () => value)
}

const arr1 = createArray(3, "x")    // T inferred as string
const arr2 = createArray(3, 42)     // T inferred as number
const arr3 = createArray<boolean>(3, true)  // Explicit T = boolean
```

Defaults are useful in generic types and React components where the most common case should not require an explicit type argument.

### When to use generics

- Your function returns a value whose type depends on the input type
- You need to constrain arguments to share a shape without fixing a concrete type
- You are building reusable utility functions, containers, or wrappers

### When to skip generics

If a concrete type is clearer, use it.

```ts
// Good — no generic needed for a fixed-purpose function.
function firstSession(sessions: readonly SessionInfo[]) {
  return sessions[0]
}
```

## Generic object helpers

### `keyof`

`keyof` gives a union of property names (the keys) for a type.

```ts
type SessionInfo = {
  id: string
  title: string
  createdAt: number
}

type SessionKey = keyof SessionInfo
// "id" | "title" | "createdAt"
// Each value is a string literal matching a property name.
```

Use `keyof` to create safe property access helpers:

```ts
function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(object: T, key: K): T[K] {
  // K extends keyof T means "K is one of T's property names."
  // T[K] means "the type of that property in T."
  return object[key]
}

const session: SessionInfo = { id: "ses_1", title: "Fix tests", createdAt: 1700000000 }

const title = getProperty(session, "title")
// TypeScript infers: K = "title", T[K] = string.

const createdAt = getProperty(session, "createdAt")
// T[K] = number.
```

If you pass a key that does not exist on the object, TypeScript rejects it at compile time:

```ts
// getProperty(session, "missing")
//              ~~~~~~~~~ Error: Argument of type '"missing"' is not assignable
//                        to parameter of type 'keyof SessionInfo'.
```

### `keyof` with `typeof`

You can combine `keyof` with `typeof` to get keys from a concrete value:

```ts
const config = {
  provider: "openai",
  model: "gpt-5",
} as const

type ConfigKey = keyof typeof config
// "provider" | "model"
```

### Using keyof for a `pluck` helper

```ts
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][] {
  // Returns an array of the values for key K from every item.
  return items.map((item) => item[key])
}

const sessions: SessionInfo[] = [
  { id: "s1", title: "Fix tests", createdAt: 1 },
  { id: "s2", title: "Add feature", createdAt: 2 },
]

const titles = pluck(sessions, "title")
// TypeScript infers: K = "title", so titles is string[].

const createdAts = pluck(sessions, "createdAt")
// createdAts is number[].
```

## Indexed access types

Use indexed access (bracket notation) to reuse a property type without redefining it.

```ts
type SessionInfo = {
  id: string
  title: string
  createdAt: number
}

type SessionID = SessionInfo["id"]
// SessionID is string — matches the type of the id property.

type SessionMeta = SessionInfo["id" | "title"]
// "id" | "title" -> SessionMeta is string (both properties are string).

type SessionKeys = SessionInfo[keyof SessionInfo]
// keyof SessionInfo is "id" | "title" | "createdAt"
// The value types are string | string | number, so SessionKeys is string | number.
```

For arrays:

```ts
type Package = {
  exports: string[]
}

type ExportName = Package["exports"][number]
// Package["exports"] is string[].
// [number] accesses the element type of that array — so ExportName is string.
```

This is particularly useful when you want to derive a type from a schema or API definition without duplicating field types:

```ts
type HandlerMap = {
  start: (input: { sessionID: string }) => void
  stop: (input: { sessionID: string; reason?: string }) => void
}

type StartHandler = HandlerMap["start"]
// (input: { sessionID: string }) => void
```

## Mapped types

Mapped types transform every property of an object type. The syntax mirrors a `for...in` loop at the type level.

```ts
type Flags<T> = {
  // [K in keyof T] iterates over every key of T.
  // The value type is boolean for every property.
  [K in keyof T]: boolean
}

type SessionInfo = {
  id: string
  title: string
  createdAt: number
}

type SessionFlags = Flags<SessionInfo>
// { id: boolean; title: boolean; createdAt: boolean }
```

### Practical variations

**Make all values nullable:**

```ts
type Nullable<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null
}

type NullableSession = Nullable<SessionInfo>
// { id: string | null; title: string | null; createdAt: number | null }
```

**Wrap all values in Promise:**

```ts
type Promised<T> = {
  [K in keyof T]: Promise<T[K]>
}

type AsyncSession = Promised<SessionInfo>
// { id: Promise<string>; title: Promise<string>; createdAt: Promise<number> }
```

### Key remapping with `as`

TypeScript 4.1+ lets you transform or filter keys with an `as` clause:

```ts
type Getters<T> = {
  // For each key K, create a new key "get" + K (capitalized).
  [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: () => T[K]
}

type SessionGetters = Getters<SessionInfo>
// { getId: () => string; getTitle: () => string; getCreatedAt: () => number }
```

You can also use `as` to **filter** keys by value type:

```ts
type StringKeys<T> = {
  // Only keep keys whose value extends string.
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K]
}

type JustStrings = StringKeys<SessionInfo>
// { id: string; title: string }
// createdAt is excluded because number does not extend string.
```

### Common built-ins

These built-in utility types are implemented using mapped types:

```ts
type PartialSession = Partial<SessionInfo>
// { id?: string; title?: string; createdAt?: number }

type RequiredSession = Required<SessionInfo>
// { id: string; title: string; createdAt: number }

type ReadonlySession = Readonly<SessionInfo>
// { readonly id: string; readonly title: string; readonly createdAt: number }
```

## Conditional types

Conditional types choose one type or another based on a condition, like a ternary at the type level.

```ts
// T extends U ? TrueBranch : FalseBranch
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"

type A = IsString<string>   // "yes"
type B = IsString<number>   // "no"
```

### Distributive conditional types

When `T` is a union, the conditional distributes over each member:

```ts
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no"

type Result = IsString<string | number>
// Evaluates each member separately:
//   IsString<string>  → "yes"
//   IsString<number>  → "no"
// Result is "yes" | "no" (union of each branch).
```

This distribution is usually what you want. If you need to prevent it, wrap both sides of `extends` in square brackets:

```ts
type IsStringNonDistributive<T> = [T] extends [string] ? "yes" : "no"

type ResultNon = IsStringNonDistributive<string | number>
// [string | number] extends [string] is false, so ResultNon is "no".
```

### Using conditional types with `never`

The `never` type is the empty union. Conditional types naturally distribute over unions, so `never` branches act as filters:

```ts
type FilterString<T> = T extends string ? T : never

type OnlyStrings = FilterString<string | number | boolean>
// Distributes:
//   FilterString<string>  → string
//   FilterString<number>  → never (filtered out)
//   FilterString<boolean> → never (filtered out)
// OnlyStrings is string.
```

In the codebase, this pattern appears in generic helpers:

```ts
type StringKeys<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K]
}
// The `as never` filters out non-string keys.
```

### Using `infer` to extract types

`infer` lets you capture a type within a conditional and give it a name. Think of it as pattern matching for types.

**Extract the element type from an array:**

```ts
type ElementOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer Item)[] ? Item : never

type Name = ElementOf<string[]>
// T = string[], which extends readonly (infer Item)[]
// Item is captured as string, so Name = string.

type First = ElementOf<[number, string]>
// Item = number | string (union of tuple elements).
```

**Extract the resolved type from a Promise:**

```ts
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer Value> ? Value : T

type A = Unwrap<Promise<string>>   // string
type B = Unwrap<string>            // string (not a promise, returned as-is)

type Nested = Unwrap<Promise<Promise<number>>>
// Only unwraps one level: Promise<number>
```

**Extract return type from a function:**

```ts
type MyReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: unknown[]) => infer R ? R : never

type Handler = (id: string) => number
type R = MyReturnType<Handler>  // number
```

In the codebase, `infer` is used to extract Effect return types, error types, and dependency types from complex service function signatures:

```ts
// Simplified pattern from service-use.ts:
type ExtractEffect<T> = T extends (...args: infer Args) => Effect.Effect<infer A, infer E, infer R>
  ? { args: Args; value: A; error: E; dependencies: R }
  : never
```

### Use conditionals carefully

Conditional types become hard to read quickly. Prefer an explicit union or overload when the type expression is simpler. Conditional types shine when a concrete type depends on a generic in a way that changes the shape of the output.

## Utility types

TypeScript provides built-in utility types for common transformations:

| Utility | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `Partial<T>` | make all properties optional | `Partial<Config>` |
| `Required<T>` | make all properties required | `Required<Options>` |
| `Readonly<T>` | make all properties readonly | `Readonly<State>` |
| `Pick<T, K>` | keep only selected keys | `Pick<Event, "type" \| "id">` |
| `Omit<T, K>` | remove selected keys | `Omit<Event, "timestamp">` |
| `Record<K, V>` | object with keys K and values V | `Record<string, Session>` |
| `ReturnType<F>` | return type of a function | `ReturnType<typeof handler>` |
| `Parameters<F>` | tuple of function parameter types | `Parameters<typeof handler>` |
| `Awaited<T>` | unwrap promise-like types | `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>` |
| `NonNullable<T>` | remove `null` and `undefined` | `NonNullable<string \| undefined>` |

### Practical compositions

```ts
type SessionInfo = {
  id: string
  title: string
  createdAt: number
  internal: string
}

// Keep only public-facing fields.
type PublicSession = Pick<SessionInfo, "id" | "title">
// { id: string; title: string }

// Make all fields optional except id.
type SessionPatch = Partial<Omit<SessionInfo, "id">>
// { title?: string; createdAt?: number; internal?: string }

// A lookup table keyed by string.
type SessionsByID = Record<string, SessionInfo>
// { [key: string]: SessionInfo }

// Extract the return type of an async function step by step.
type Loaded = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchConfig>>
// Step 1: typeof fetchConfig  → the function type
// Step 2: ReturnType<...>     → the return type (a Promise)
// Step 3: Awaited<...>        → the unwrapped value type
```

### Pick vs Omit

```ts
// Pick: "I want these fields."
type Summary = Pick<SessionInfo, "id" | "title">

// Omit: "I want everything except these."
type WithoutInternal = Omit<SessionInfo, "internal">

// These produce the same type when the sets are complements.
```

## `typeof` in type positions

Runtime `typeof` checks values. TypeScript `typeof` in a type position extracts a value's type.

```ts
const defaultConfig = {
  provider: "openai",
  model: "gpt-5",
}

type Config = typeof defaultConfig
```

This is common with schema values.

```ts
const Agent = Schema.Struct({
  id: Schema.String,
  name: Schema.String,
})

type Agent = Schema.Schema.Type<typeof Agent>
```

## `as const`

`as const` preserves literal types and readonly structure.

```ts
const modes = ["steer", "queue"] as const

type Mode = (typeof modes)[number]
```

Without `as const`, `modes` is just `string[]`.

Use it for fixed tables and literal registries.

```ts
const routes = {
  health: "/health",
  events: "/events",
} as const

type RouteName = keyof typeof routes
```

## `satisfies` vs `as const`

Both keywords preserve type information but serve different purposes. Understanding when to use each — and when to use both together — will make your type definitions more precise.

### What `as const` does

`as const` tells TypeScript to infer the most specific literal types and make the value readonly.

```ts
const modes = ["steer", "queue"] as const
// TypeScript infers: readonly ["steer", "queue"]
// Without as const, it would infer: string[]

const routes = {
  health: "/health",
  events: "/events",
} as const
// TypeScript infers:
// { readonly health: "/health"; readonly events: "/events" }
// Without as const, the values would be string and properties would be mutable.
```

### What `satisfies` does

`satisfies` checks that a value conforms to a type without widening the value's own type.

```ts
type ProviderConfig = {
  id: string
  models: readonly string[]
}

const provider = {
  id: "openai",
  models: ["gpt-5", "gpt-5-mini"],
} satisfies ProviderConfig

// The models array keeps its literal tuple type:
// readonly ["gpt-5", "gpt-5-mini"]
// Without satisfies, models would be string[].
// With a type annotation (: ProviderConfig), models would also be string[].
```

### When to use each

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Preserve literal types AND make everything readonly | `as const` |
| Check shape without changing inferred types | `satisfies` |
| Both: check a constant's shape AND preserve its literals | `as const satisfies` |

### Using both together

```ts
type ProviderConfig = {
  id: string
  models: readonly string[]
}

const openai = {
  id: "openai-1",
  models: ["gpt-5", "gpt-5-mini"],
} as const satisfies ProviderConfig

// as const: makes "openai-1" the literal type, and the array readonly.
// satisfies: checks the shape matches ProviderConfig without widening.

type ProviderID = typeof openai["id"]
// "openai-1" (literal, thanks to as const)
```

This pattern is common in the codebase for config tables and registries where you want the precision of literal types and the safety of shape checking.

## Branded types

Branded types distinguish strings that have different meanings.

```ts
type SessionID = string & { readonly __brand: "SessionID" }
// The intersection with { readonly __brand } creates a nominal type.
// SessionID is assignable to string, but string is not assignable to SessionID.

type MessageID = string & { readonly __brand: "MessageID" }

function loadSession(id: SessionID) {
  return id
}

// loadSession(someMessageID)
// ~~~~~~~~~~ Type error: Argument of type 'MessageID' is not assignable
//            to parameter of type 'SessionID'.
```

Effect Schema has first-class support for brands.

```ts
export const ID = Schema.String.pipe(
  Schema.brand("Session.ID"),
)
// The brand carries through Effect's type system — Schema.Type<typeof ID>
// resolves to a branded string that prevents mix-ups at compile time.

export interface ID extends Schema.Schema.Type<typeof ID> {}
```

Brands prevent accidentally passing a message ID where a session ID is expected.

## Template literal types

TypeScript can model string patterns using template literal syntax. This is useful for route patterns, event names, and other structured string formats.

```ts
type PackagePath = `packages/${string}`
// Matches any string starting with "packages/".

const path: PackagePath = "packages/core"      // OK
// const bad: PackagePath = "src/core"         // Error
```

### Inferring from string patterns

With `infer` in a template literal, you can extract parts of a string at the type level:

```ts
type ExtractID<T> = T extends `/sessions/${infer ID}` ? ID : never

type A = ExtractID<"/sessions/ses_1">
// ID = "ses_1", so A is "ses_1".

type B = ExtractID<"/health">
// Does not match the pattern, so B is never.
```

### Practical example: route parameters

```ts
type Route = `/sessions/${string}/messages/${string}`

type ExtractParams<T> = T extends `/sessions/${infer SessionID}/messages/${infer MessageID}`
  ? { sessionID: SessionID; messageID: MessageID }
  : never

type Params = ExtractParams<"/sessions/ses_1/messages/msg_2">
// { sessionID: "ses_1"; messageID: "msg_2" }
```

Template literal types are most useful when you have a fixed pattern and need to enforce or extract parts of it at compile time. For arbitrary input strings, runtime validation is still required.

## Recursive types

A type that references itself in its definition is a recursive type. They are useful for nested data structures like JSON, trees, and configuration objects.

```ts
type JSONValue =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | null
  | JSONValue[]           // An array of JSON values — notice the self-reference.
  | { [key: string]: JSONValue }  // An object whose values are all JSON values.

// Now any valid JSON document is typed:
const data: JSONValue = {
  name: "config",
  version: 2,
  nested: {
    enabled: true,
    items: [1, "two", null],
  },
}
```

Recursive types are also useful for nested configs:

```ts
type PluginConfig = {
  name: string
  enabled: boolean
  children?: PluginConfig[]  // Plugins can contain sub-plugins.
}

const config: PluginConfig = {
  name: "root",
  enabled: true,
  children: [
    { name: "sub", enabled: false },
  ],
}
```

TypeScript has a recursion depth limit (typically ~50 levels) to prevent infinite type evaluation. In practice, this is rarely a problem.

## Declaration files

`.d.ts` files describe types for JavaScript code or generated output. Generate them with `tsc` rather than writing them by hand. In this repo, many packages export TypeScript source directly and typecheck with package-local configs.

When a package exposes public APIs, its `exports` map and TypeScript declarations determine how other packages import it.

## Function overloads

A function can have multiple call signatures (overloads) when the return type depends on the argument types in a way that generics cannot express.

```ts
// Overload signatures (no body):
function create(input: string): SessionInfo
function create(input: SessionInfo): SessionInfo

// Implementation signature (with body):
function create(input: string | SessionInfo): SessionInfo {
  if (typeof input === "string") {
    return { id: input, title: input, createdAt: Date.now() }
  }
  return input
}
```

The overload signatures sit above the implementation. When you call `create`, TypeScript tries the overloads in order. The implementation signature is not visible to callers — it only needs to be broad enough to cover all overloads.

In this codebase, overloads are used sparingly (for example, in error construction where different argument types produce the same result type). Prefer generics or discriminated unions when they can express the relationship more clearly.

```ts
// Prefer generics when possible — they express the relationship directly:
function duplicate<T>(value: T): T {
  return value
}
```

### Other rarely-seen patterns

**Abstract classes** (2 files in the codebase) have abstract methods that subclasses must implement:

```ts
abstract class NamedError extends Error {
  abstract schema(): Schema.Top
}
```

**Enum** (4 declarations in 2 files, LSP code):

```ts
enum SymbolKind { File = 1, Module = 2 }
```

The codebase generally prefers literal unions over enums. Use enums only when interacting with APIs that define them (like LSP).

**Visibility keywords** on class fields:

```ts
class Handler {
  private readonly abort = new AbortController()
  protected mcpName: string
}
```

Most of the codebase avoids classes in favor of Effect service patterns, so you are unlikely to need `private` or `abstract` in new code.

## Module resolution

This repo uses Bun and bundler-style TypeScript resolution in frontend packages. Package `exports` and `imports` maps matter.

```json
{
  "type": "module",     // Use ES module resolution (not CommonJS).
  "exports": {
    "./*": "./src/*.ts" // Map any import within the package to the source file.
  },
  "imports": {
    "#sqlite": {                   // Private import alias (starts with #).
      "bun": "./src/sqlite.bun.ts",  // Resolved by Bun.
      "node": "./src/sqlite.node.ts" // Resolved by Node.js.
    }
  }
}
```

The import path is part of the package API.

## Type-only imports

Use `import type` when importing only types.

```ts
import type { SessionInfo } from "./session"
// type-only import: erased at compile time, no runtime dependency.
import { formatSession } from "./format"
// value import: creates a runtime dependency.
```

Type-only imports disappear from emitted JavaScript and avoid accidental runtime dependencies.

## Avoiding circular runtime dependencies

Types can sometimes be imported without runtime cost, but value imports create runtime dependencies. The repo dependency rule matters:

- Schema can feed Core and Protocol.
- Core and Protocol can feed Server.
- Client runtime code can depend on Schema and Protocol.
- Client runtime code must not depend on Core or Server.
- `sdk-next` composes Client, Core, and Server.

## When advanced types are worth it

Advanced types are useful when they keep two pieces of code linked so they cannot drift. They are less useful when they make the reader solve a puzzle before understanding the program. In this repo, good uses tend to be registries, generated/protocol-adjacent shapes, branded IDs, and helpers that preserve relationships.

```ts
const statusLabels = {
  idle: "Idle",
  running: "Running",
  failed: "Failed",
} as const  // Without as const, values would be string and Status would be string.

type Status = keyof typeof statusLabels
// "idle" | "running" | "failed" (narrow literal keys).

function labelStatus(status: Status) {
  // The key type and table stay linked — if you add a new status to the table,
  // the type automatically includes the new key. No separate enum to update.
  return statusLabels[status]
}
```

Avoid using conditional or mapped types just to avoid writing a small explicit type. If the type is harder to read than the value it describes, prefer the explicit type.

## Reading a complex type

When a type looks dense, read it from the value outward.

```ts
const handlers = {
  start: (input: { sessionID: string }) => input.sessionID,
  stop: (input: { sessionID: string; reason?: string }) => input.reason ?? "done",
} as const  // Preserves literal types so typeof handlers has the exact function signatures.

type HandlerName = keyof typeof handlers
// Step 1: typeof handlers -> the object type with literal keys.
// Step 2: keyof -> "start" | "stop".

type HandlerInput<Name extends HandlerName> = Parameters<(typeof handlers)[Name]>[0]
// Step 3: (typeof handlers)[Name] -> select one function by key.
// Step 4: Parameters<...> -> tuple of parameter types.
// Step 5: [0] -> first parameter (the input object).
```

Read it in this order:

1. `handlers` is the runtime table.
2. `typeof handlers` turns that value into a type.
3. `keyof typeof handlers` produces `"start" | "stop"`.
4. `(typeof handlers)[Name]` selects one function from the table.
5. `Parameters<...>[0]` extracts that function's first argument.

If the type protects a real table, registry, generated contract, or branded boundary, it is usually worth learning. If it only hides a small local object shape, write the shape directly.

## Putting it together: typed plugin registry

This example composes generics, branded types, `as const`, `satisfies`, and conditional types into a realistic plugin registry.

```ts
// Step 1: Define the plugin contract with generics.
type Plugin<Config extends Record<string, unknown> = Record<string, unknown>> = {
  name: string
  enabled: boolean
  config: Config
  handler: (config: Config) => Effect.Effect<void>
}

// Step 2: Branded IDs prevent mixing up plugin identifiers.
type PluginID = string & { readonly __brand: "PluginID" }

function pluginID(value: string): PluginID {
  return value as PluginID
}

// Step 3: Define concrete plugin types with as const + satisfies.
type CodePlugin = Plugin<{ model: string; maxTokens?: number }>
type DatabasePlugin = Plugin<{ url: string; poolSize: number }>

const codePlugin = {
  name: "code-review",
  enabled: true,
  config: { model: "gpt-5", maxTokens: 4096 },
  handler: (config) => Effect.sync(() => console.log(config.model)),
} as const satisfies CodePlugin

// as const preserves the literal "code-review" for the name.
// satisfies checks the shape matches CodePlugin without widening.

const dbPlugin = {
  name: "database",
  enabled: false,
  config: { url: "postgres://localhost", poolSize: 10 },
  handler: (config) => Effect.sync(() => console.log(config.url)),
} as const satisfies DatabasePlugin

// Step 4: Registry with a mapped type to extract handler return types.
type PluginRegistry = Record<string, Plugin>

type HandlerReturn<T> = T extends Plugin<infer C>
  ? ReturnType<T["handler"]>
  : never

type CodeHandlerReturn = HandlerReturn<typeof codePlugin>
// Extract the Effect type from the handler.
```

The composed result: branded ID types prevent passing an arbitrary string where a plugin ID is expected. `as const` preserves literal names for keyof lookups. `satisfies` ensures each plugin matches its contract without widening away useful literals. Conditional types with `infer` extract handler return types automatically.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not outsmart the code

The best TypeScript type makes the runtime code easier to change safely. If a type requires a long explanation but protects little real behavior, it is probably too clever for handbook-level project code.
:::

## Recap

- Generics preserve relationships.
- `keyof` and indexed access reuse object structure.
- Mapped and conditional types power utility types.
- `as const` keeps literals.
- `satisfies` checks shape without losing precision.
- Brands prevent mixing semantically different strings.
- Type-only imports help protect runtime dependency boundaries.
